sens: Message or command communicated by a messenger on behalf of the one who sends him
Official and solemn word that someone transmits in the name of an authority
H4400.detail:
1. This word refers to the message that a messenger conveys on behalf of his master or the one who sent him. It is the official word entrusted to someone to faithfully report to others. In Haggai 1:13, Haggai, acting as a messenger of the Lord, communicates to the people the order or message of the Lord: this shows that he adds nothing of his own, but transmits exactly what God commanded him to say.
2. More broadly, it is a word that carries authority, demanding obedience because it comes from a higher authority (a king, God, a master). It is not a mere suggestion, but an instruction or command to be executed.
H4400.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that refers to the idea of "message" or "communicated word." The form with the suffix "-ut" makes it an abstract noun, designating the action or quality itself. It is the type of word that a *malakh* (messenger, angel) carries from one place to another: a word with a mission, charged with authority.
H4400.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Haggai 1:13. In this context, the prophet Haggai has just spoken to the people, and the text specifies that he did so "according to the order of the Lord." Haggai does not act on his own: he is the spokesperson for God, and the message he delivers is the one that God entrusted to him. This unique context shows that the term emphasizes the official, authorized, and binding nature of the prophetic message.
H4400.portee: This word reminds the reader that when God speaks through his prophets, it is not a personal opinion, but a message with divine authority behind it. Understanding that Haggai speaks "according to the order of the Lord" reinforces the seriousness of the call to rebuild the Temple: it is a divine command, not a suggestion. This encourages us to receive the prophetic word with respect and obedience.

sens: The prophet whose name means "My messenger"
Author of the last book of the Old Testament
H4401.detail: Malachi is a prophet from the time of exile and return, whose Hebrew name literally means "My messenger." He is known only through the book that bears his name, where his signature is found in verse 1:1: "Oracle, word of the Lord to Israel by Malachi." He is the last of the twelve minor prophets of the Hebrew Bible, and thus the last book of the Old Testament. No other biographical details about his life have come down to us.
H4401.origine: The Hebrew name Malachi (מַלְאָכִי) is composed of two elements: "mal" (messenger, angel) and "i" (my, possessive). It therefore means "My messenger" — a name that emphasizes the role of the prophet as God's spokesperson sent to his people. This name perfectly reflects the prophetic mission: to convey the message of the Lord to Israel.
H4401.emploi: Malachi appears only once in the Bible, in Malachi 1:1, where he identifies himself as the prophet who received the word of the Lord for Israel. He is the author of the last book of the Old Testament, composed of four chapters. His time is that of the return from exile, probably in the 5th century B.C. Unlike many prophets of the Old Testament, no other information about his life, genealogy, or personal context is conveyed by Scripture.

sens: Fullness, richness, generous quantity
State of one who has everything in profusion
Context of flourishing and well-being
H4402.detail: 1. The word denotes a fullness, an abundance — the idea of being filled, lacking nothing. In Song of Solomon 5:12, the beloved's eyes are compared to doves "by the streams, bathing in milk, resting in the midst of abundance": the image is of happy, well-fed creatures in an environment of wealth and satisfaction. 2. More broadly, the word evokes a state of prosperity and generous provision, a context where life flourishes without lack or restriction.
H4402.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to fill" or "to be full." It belongs to the family of terms that describe fullness and satisfaction, the idea of completeness. Its etymology refers to the concrete image of a container or space filled to overflowing.
H4402.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Song of Solomon 5:12. It is found in a poetic description of the beloved's features, where abundance serves as a metaphor to evoke happy life and flourishing. Its context is clearly lyrical and romantic, celebrating beauty and fullness.
H4402.portee: This word invites the reader to contemplate abundance as a source of beauty and good life. In the biblical text, it reminds us that satisfaction and prosperity are goods that God offers, and that material and spiritual wealth can be an opportunity for shared joy and mutual flourishing.

sens: Piece or set of fabric worn to cover and protect oneself
Garment worn during ceremonies or to fulfill a function
Prestigious adornment that manifests rank or wealth
Blood or substance that stains a garment
H4403.detail:
1. The garment is primarily the fabric or clothing worn on the body for covering and protection. The word can refer to a single garment or multiple garments together: in 1 Kings 10:5, the garments of those who served King Solomon are enumerated, meaning their service clothes.
2. The word takes on a solemn nuance when it comes to garments of function: in 2 Kings 10:22, "garments are brought out" for the servants of Baal, meaning they are provided with the ritual clothes they must wear to perform their worship.
3. Garments can also express wealth, beauty, and royal status. In Ezekiel 16:13, the woman is "dressed in fine linen, silk, and embroidered fabrics": her garments tell of her opulence and honor, they are adornments of gold and silver.
4. Finally, a garment can be stained or marked by blood and violence: in Isaiah 63:3, the prophet speaks of blood splattered on his garments during judgment — the garment then becomes a witness to the action performed.
H4403.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to clothe" or "to cover." It is constructed as an action noun ("that which clothes"), like many Hebrew nouns formed from a verb. Words from the same family denote the act of putting on a garment or covering oneself. It is a simple and common word in biblical Hebrew, which speaks of a daily reality: every Israelite wore clothing, and the Bible often mentions garments as signs of status, ritual, or transformation.
H4403.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical books and the prophets. In 1 Kings 10:5 and 2 Chronicles 9:4, it refers to the official garments worn by the servants of King Solomon, a detail that impresses the Queen of Sheba. In 2 Kings 10:22, it is the term for the sacred garments of Baal worship. Job 27:16 metaphorically compares amassed garments to mud, to show the absurdity of wealth. Isaiah 63:3 and Ezekiel 16:13 use the word figuratively: one to express the stain of judgment, the other to symbolize adornment and glory. Throughout all these uses, the garment is never a detail: it is what covers the body and what shows it to others.
H4403.portee: The garment reminds us that the human body is real and that it needs to be covered and protected. The Bible does not ignore the body by covering it: it recognizes dignity and modesty. Garments also speak of rank, function, and glory of a person — what one wears says who one is. But the garment can also be stained or torn, reminding us that all that shines outwardly can be marked or brought low by God's judgment.

sens: Installation where bricks are baked
Mold or workspace for shaping bricks
Yard or quadrangle adjacent to a brick factory
H4404.detail:
1. It is the installation, generally outdoors or semi-covered, where raw bricks are baked. In 2 Samuel 12:31, David forces the inhabitants of the Ammonite cities to work in these kilns, a grueling task symbolic of enslavement. The brick kiln was an essential element of the urban and military infrastructure of the ancient Near East.

2. The word can also refer to the mold or space where clay is shaped before firing, or the site itself where this work takes place. Jeremiah hides stones "in the clay of the brick kiln" at Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:9), evoking the malleable clay prepared there.

3. By extension, it refers to the courtyard or square space (quadrangle) that surrounds or makes up the production site. Nahum 3:14 calls on Nineveh to "restore the brick kiln," an image of reconstruction and mobilization of resources in times of threat.
H4404.origine: The Hebrew word mal.ben comes from the verb "to make" (עשה, asah) and "brick" (לְבֵן, leben). It literally designates the place of brick making. The brick is the primary raw material of Mesopotamian and Levantine construction, hence the importance of the kiln that allowed them to be baked. It is a specialized term related to archaeology and the building industry.
H4404.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the singular, in contexts of forced labor, siege, or defense. In 2 Samuel 12:31, David subjects the Ammonite populations to work in the brick kilns, a humiliating and exhausting task. In Jeremiah 43:9, the prophet symbolically hides stones in the clay of the kiln at Tahpanhes, an Egyptian city. In Nahum 3:14, it is a sarcastic call to Nineveh to strengthen its military and civilian facilities in the face of invasion. The word always designates a real and concrete architectural installation, a foundation of power and resistance.
H4404.portee: This word reminds us that the humble work of construction carried the civilization of the biblical world, but also that empires imposed it through domination. It invites the reader to see in the bricks and their kilns the image of human enslavement and resilience.

sens: What is said, what comes out of the mouth
Expression, manner of speaking
Discourse, set of words
Promise, commitment stated
Subject of conversation, remarks
H4405.detail:
1. The word is primarily what comes out of a person's mouth when they speak. It is the word, the phrase, the concrete statement. In 2 Samuel 23:2, David says that the word of the Lord rests on his tongue — it is the word that God entrusts to him to pronounce.
2. It is also the manner in which one expresses oneself, the way of speaking unique to each person. Job 12:11 compares the ear that discerns words to the palate that savors food: one evaluates the quality of a word as one evaluates that of a dish.
3. The word designates a discourse, a set of words spoken to convince or instruct. In Job 34:2, Job invites the wise to listen to his discourse.
4. A word can be a commitment, something one promises to do or uphold. It then carries the weight of a promise.
5. It is also simply the subject being discussed, what is talked about. In Job 18:2, one asks when this discourse will end — that is, this endless conversation.
H4405.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to say," "to speak." It is close to the Aramaic word מִלָּה (millah), which has exactly the same meaning. In the Hebrew lexicon, the word (milah) is what springs from a person's speech (dabar in more common Hebrew), but with a nuance: milah emphasizes the phonetic, sound aspect, what is actually pronounced. It is the word "spoken" rather than simply "said."
H4405.emploi: This word appears 38 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the book of Job (about 30 occurrences). In this context, it is a central term of dialogue: Job's interlocutors exchange words, dispute over the best words, invoke the wisdom contained in the words. In 2 Samuel 23:2, the word of the Lord signifies the divine revelation pronounced by the prophet. The word always emphasizes the concrete and sound aspect: what is said, what is stated, what fills the air and the ear. That is why one can have "a cut-off word" (Job 32:15) — literally, the words are interrupted, one no longer dares to speak.
H4405.portee: For the believer, this entry reminds us that words carry weight. What we say is not neutral: it is an act that comes from us and reaches others. The word of the Lord proclaimed by the prophet is the very revelation of God. Likewise, our words reflect who we are and engage our responsibility. The care given to words — their listening, their discernment — is a form of wisdom.

sens: A statement, what is said
An order, an instruction
A matter, a question, a subject
The interpretation or explanation of a thing
H4406.detail:
1. The word is primarily what is pronounced, a statement that comes from the mouth. In Daniel 7:11, the king sees a beast that utters "arrogant words": these words are proud statements. It is the thought formulated in words.
2. The word can also be an order, an instruction given with authority. In Daniel 3:22, the "order" of King Nebuchadnezzar to increase the fire of the furnace is called a word: something that commands, that must be obeyed.
3. The word also designates a matter, a question, a subject being dealt with. In Daniel 2:10, when the Chaldeans say "the thing that the king asks for," they are talking about what needs to be accomplished, the task, the question posed.
4. Finally, the word can be an explanation or interpretation. In Daniel 5:26, "the interpretation of these words" is the word that reveals the meaning of the mysterious writing. It is the message that sheds light.
H4406.origine: This Aramaic word comes from a very ancient root meaning "to speak," "to pronounce." The corresponding Hebrew word is "dabar" (דָּבָר), extremely common in the Old Testament. As in Hebrew, the word extends from the concrete meaning (what is said) to the broader sense (a matter, a thing). The word carries the idea that speech is an action: when one speaks, one does something.
H4406.emploi: This word appears 22 times in the book of Daniel, always in Aramaic, the dialect used for chapters 2 to 7. It mainly designates what King Nebuchadnezzar says or commands: his words, his orders, his demands. It is also found for the words of the Chaldeans, of Daniel, and the very words of God. The word often appears in the plural (“words”) to evoke a discourse, a succession of statements. Its use is very broad: it adapts to the context, from precise command to vague matter, from historical speech to divine decree.
H4406.portee: Reading this word, one understands that speech is never just an empty sound. In Daniel, the king's words determine the fate of men, the words of the mysterious writer fix the course of history, and the words of Daniel reveal God's will. For the Christian reader, this reminds us that words carry weight, that they build or destroy, that they engage. This is true of human words, and even more so of the word of God.

sens: Man of the time of the return from exile, father or member of a family from Judah
H4409I.detail: Malluc is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the return from exile after the Babylonian captivity. He appears in the list of men who ended their mixed marriages with foreign women, on the order of the priest Ezra (Ezra 10:32). His name appears alongside that of Shemariah, likely relatives or members of the same family, in the clan of Benjamin.
H4409I.origine: The name Malluc (or Melicu as a variant) means "counselor" or "one who gives counsel," formed from a Semitic root denoting counsel or advice. It is a name borne by Israelites of the return period, particularly among the descendants of Judah who returned from Babylon.
H4409I.emploi: Malluc appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:32, where he is cited in the list of Israelites who repudiated their foreign wives after the return from exile, around 458 B.C. This list was of great importance to Ezra, who sought to purify the people and restore their separation from neighboring nations. The context shows that Malluc was a man of sufficient status or importance to be specifically mentioned in this record.

sens: priest who returned from exile with Zerubbabel
H4409J.detail: Malluc is a priest who participated in the return from exile to Jerusalem under the leadership of Zerubbabel, during the time of the temple's reconstruction. The text of Nehemiah mentions him among the leaders of the priests who sealed the covenant with God (Nehemiah 10:4), confirming his important place in the priestly hierarchy of the time. His name also appears in the list of chief priests of paternal houses (Nehemiah 12:2), showing that he founded a priestly lineage that endured beyond his generation.
H4409J.origine: The Hebrew name מַלּוּךְ literally means "counselor" or "one who deliberates," derived from a root evoking counsel and reflection. This name was borne by men of status, notably priests and leaders, which fits perfectly for a priestly chief. The text also notes a variant called Mallichi (מְלִיכוּ), which likely designates a descendant or successor of the same man in the priestly lineage.
H4409J.emploi: Malluc appears twice in the book of Nehemiah, both during the time of the return from exile (around 520 B.C.). He is mentioned among the leaders of the priests who sign the covenant document in Nehemiah 10:4, where he is listed alongside other prestigious names like Hattush and Shebaniah. In the parallel list of Nehemiah 12:2, his name is found among the chief priests of paternal houses, indicating that he represented an established priestly house with enough prestige to be named after him. These two mentions demonstrate the lasting importance of Malluc in the priestly institution rebuilt after the exile.

sens: The exercise of royal power, the authority of a king over his people
The dignity and status of a king
The entirety of the territory and subjects under a king
The right to reign, transmitted or entrusted by God
The dominion, the sovereignty established by royal power
H4410.detail:
1. The royalty is primarily the concrete exercise of royal power: Saul "took possession of the royalty over Israel" (1 Samuel 14:47), meaning he began to reign and govern effectively.
2. It also refers to the dignity and royal status itself, which makes one a king: when Jezebel says to Ahab, "Is it you now who exercises sovereignty over Israel?" (1 Kings 21:7), she speaks of this sacred charge.
3. Royalty can also represent the reign in its entirety, as a possession and a good: "the Lord has delivered the kingdom into the hands of Absalom" (2 Samuel 16:8) means that all royal power has changed hands.
4. It is also the right or the right to reign, recognized and established: when one asks for the "royalty" for a prince (1 Kings 2:22), one is claiming the right to succeed to the throne.
5. Finally, it expresses absolute sovereignty: "To the Lord belongs the reign" (Psalms 22:29) means that God possesses supreme authority over all nations.
H4410.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root "malak" which means "to be king" or "to reign." Royalty is therefore literally "the state or function of one who reigns." The same root produces "melek" (king) and other terms related to royal power in Hebrew. In the texts, this word expresses not only status but also the idea that Israel recognized royalty as a divine institution: the king represented God among his people.
H4410.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) where it recounts the establishment of royalty in Israel. It also appears in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel) and the Psalms. The usages show that royalty is a political reality: it is acquired (Saul "takes" it), lost (Saul loses it to David), transmitted (from David to his sons), and defended (wars and revolts). But it is also theological: "the Lord has delivered the kingdom" indicates that God controls the granting of royal power. The prophets use this term to express both human dominion and God's ultimate sovereignty.
H4410.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that royalty, in Israel and throughout the world, ultimately belongs to God. It is never absolute or independent: it is a mandate received from God, a responsibility towards Him and towards the people. The Bible shows that the kings of Israel often failed by forgetting this truth. This sheds light on the promise of an eternal King (the Messiah) whose reign will be just and unshakeable, unlike human royalties that pass away.

sens: place where one stops to spend the night while traveling
inn, lodge, temporary accommodation
end, tip of a territory
H4411.detail:
1. The word designates the place where a traveler stops to sleep during his journey. It is a place of rest and halt, generally located on a road or by a river. In Genesis 42:27 and 43:21, Joseph's brothers discover the money in their sacks at the "place" where they spent the night while descending from Egypt.
2. The word can also refer to an inn, a khan, or any rudimentary lodging establishment where travelers find refuge. It particularly evokes the image of minimum comfort offered in the desert or on ancient roads.
3. By extension, the word can mean the end or tip of something, as in 2 Kings 19:23 where it designates the "last" peak of Lebanon, meaning its ultimate summit.
H4411.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of staying, stopping, or spending the night in a place. The same root appears in other contexts to evoke rest or halting. The basic image is that of a traveler who must interrupt his journey for the night and find shelter.
H4411.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in travel narratives. In Genesis and Exodus, it describes the places where the patriarchs and Moses rest at night (Genesis 42:27, Exodus 4:24). Joshua uses it for the temporary camp of the people (Joshua 4:3 and 4:8). In 2 Kings 19:23, it takes on the meaning of "summit" or "end." The context always shows a halt, a temporary rest, or a geographical limit.
H4411.portee: This word reminds the reader that biblical travels were not mere journeys, but difficult undertakings where one had to rest and sleep along the way. It anchors the narratives in the concrete reality of ancient travel and shows the fatigue of travelers, even during great events of salvation — such as the descent into Egypt or the crossing of the desert.

sens: small light shelter, temporary or fragile construction
humble and isolated dwelling
unstable or precarious thing
H4412.detail:
1. A hut is a small, lightweight, and simple building, quickly constructed to provide temporary shelter. It is the shelter that the keeper of vineyards or cucumber fields sets up during harvests to watch over the crops: Isaiah 1:8 speaks of a "hut in a cucumber field."
2. Figuratively, a hut refers to any humble and isolated dwelling, or even the condition of one who seeks refuge there: Jerusalem, once glorious, is reduced to the state of a small hut, fragile and solitary amid ruins.
3. The word especially evokes fragility and instability: Isaiah 24:20 compares the earth that staggers to a hut that wobbles, to show how it becomes unstable under the weight of sin, ready to collapse.
H4412.origine: The Hebrew word מְלוּנָה comes from a root meaning "to stay, to dwell," but with the idea of a temporary or rudimentary dwelling. Its original image is that of a transient lodging, a shelter that one merely passes through or that lasts only a short time. In the Old Testament, this word contrasts with solid and permanent houses.
H4412.emploi: This Hebrew word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Isaiah. In both cases, it designates a fragile structure compared to something larger or normal. In Isaiah 1:8, it is the concrete shelter of the field, illustrating how Jerusalem found itself alone and stripped. In Isaiah 24:20, the hut becomes an image of cosmic instability and divine judgment: the whole earth, under the weight of iniquity, staggers like a frail cabin.
H4412.portee: This word reminds us that our earthly dwellings and human constructions are fragile before God. It also invites us to meditate on the vulnerability of this world in the face of divine judgment and the weight of sin. For the believer, it emphasizes that only what is built on God is stable.

sens: One of the fourteen sons of the musician Heman during the time of King David
A chief of a Levitical family responsible for temple service
H4413.detail:
1. Mallothi is one of the fourteen sons of Heman, an important musician in the service of King David. His name appears in the list of Heman's sons in 1 Chronicles 25:4, alongside his brothers Bukkijah, Mattaniah, Uziel, and ten others.
2. Mallothi is given a role in temple worship: he is chosen by lot to lead a group of Levitical musicians during divine service. In 1 Chronicles 25:26, he is named among the family heads responsible for organizing worship, with his sons and brothers, forming a group of twelve people.
H4413.origine: The name Mallothi means "I have spoken" or "I have uttered" in Hebrew (from the root נלל, which evokes the action of pronouncing or emitting a word). This name is particularly fitting for a son of a musician and poet, since Heman himself is described in the Psalms as a wise man whose wisdom is expressed through song and music.
H4413.emploi: Mallothi is mentioned twice in 1 Chronicles 25, which describes the organization of Levitical musicians in the temple under King David. He appears in the genealogical list of Heman's sons (25:4), and then in the record of the drawing of lots (25:26), where he is assigned to the nineteenth place in the service cycle. No other biographical details are provided in the Scriptures.

sens: To disappear by dispersing, like smoke that dissipates
To be reduced to nothing, annihilated
H4414A.detail:
1. The verb evokes the image of smoke that disperses and vanishes into the air, or of a garment that falls into tatters and disintegrates — something that decomposes, disunites, loses its cohesion, and gradually disappears. Isaiah uses this word to describe how the heavens themselves, despite their vastness and apparent permanence, will vanish like smoke before God (Isaiah 51:6).
2. Figuratively, it means to be annihilated, to disappear completely. The word emphasizes not just a simple erasure, but a disintegration: the inhabitants of the earth will perish like flies, in other words, will be reduced to nothing in the face of God's eternal justice and salvation, which will never falter.
H4414A.origine: The Hebrew verb mālach comes from a root that evokes the idea of dispersing, dissolving. Its basic image is that of something that detaches, scatters, falls apart — like a fabric that tears or a substance that vaporizes. This root belongs to the family of verbs of annihilation and disintegration.
H4414A.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 51:6, in a discourse of consolation from the Lord to Israel. God affirms that even the most stable and impressive realities in the eyes of men — heaven and earth — will eventually vanish, while His salvation and justice will remain forever. The use of the Niphal (passive or reflexive form) reinforces the idea of an inevitable and complete disappearance: it is a settled matter, a sealed fate.
H4414A.portee: This word reminds the believer that everything that seems solid, durable, and impressive in this world — powers, material realities, human institutions — is actually temporary and destined to vanish. Only God's salvation and justice are eternal and trustworthy. It is an invitation not to place our hope in what can disappear, but in the word of God that endures forever.

sens: To season food with salt
To rub or wash a surface with salt
To add salt for purification or preservation
To mark with a covenant or pact
H4414B.detail:
1. To salt primarily means to add salt to something to enhance its flavor: the perfumer "salts" his mixture to make it more savory and lasting (Exodus 30:35).
2. It can also mean to rub or wash a surface with salt: when a baby is born, it is "salted" by being rubbed with salt for purification and cleansing (Ezekiel 16:4).
3. In a sacrificial context, salting an offering means adding salt to preserve and sanctify it, making it an act of consecration (Leviticus 2:13).
4. Salt becomes a symbol of the covenant with God: putting salt on the offering marks it with the seal of this eternal and inviolable pact.
H4414B.origine: The Hebrew verb מָלַח (malach) comes from the root מ-ל-ח which designates salt (מֶלַח, melach). Salt was a precious substance in antiquity, used to preserve food, purify, and seal agreements. The equivalent Aramaic verb literally means "to eat salt," recalling that sharing salt sealed a covenant between two people.
H4414B.emploi: This verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 30:35, it describes the seasoning of a perfume for cultic use. In Leviticus 2:13, it refers to the requirement that every sacrifice must be salted, making it a demand of worship. In Ezekiel 16:4, salt figures in the purification ritual of a newborn, a common practice in the ancient Near East. In each case, salt serves both a practical function (preservation, purification) and a symbolic one (covenant, sanctification).
H4414B.portee: Salt reminds the believer that their offering, their prayer, everything they present to God, must be marked by permanence and faithfulness. It is an invitation to live in the covenant established with God, to bear its indelible mark as salt marks whatever it touches. This simple image shows that sanctification comes through concrete actions and symbols that engage the whole body.

sens: To consume salt, the table food
Symbolically, to be employed and under the authority of the one who feeds you
H4415.detail:
1. Literally, to eat salt: this is a simple and daily act. In Ezra 4:14, the Persian officials say, "we eat the salt of the palace," meaning they are fed at the expense of the king — the royal palace provides them with food. Salt was precious and a symbol of complete nourishment provided by the master.
2. Figuratively, this expression thus means "to be in the service of someone, to receive one's sustenance from him, and to be indebted to him." Eating bread and salt with someone creates a bond of loyalty and gratitude towards the one who feeds you. This is why the officials of King Ahasuerus assert that they cannot allow the king to be dishonored: they live off his goods.
H4415.origine: This Aramaic word derives from the same root as the Hebrew מָלַח (malach, "to salt"), which expresses the action of adding salt. Aramaic borrows this notion from Hebrew, and it first designates the act of salting and then, by extension, consuming salt. Eating salt with someone or salt that someone provides has become an expression of dependence and alliance.
H4415.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 4:14. The Persian officials who collaborate in the construction of the temple report to the king that "we eat the salt of the palace," in other words, that the royal treasury feeds them. This phrase explains their interest in supporting royal authority: the one who feeds you owes you loyalty. The expression reflects a common usage in the ancient world where sharing the food and salt of a master seals the alliance between servants and sovereign.
H4415.portee: This word reminds us that faithfulness to God and to the established order that He blesses is linked to gratitude. Eating bread with someone, receiving from his hand, creates a debt of the heart. For the disciple of Jesus, this also sheds light on the sacrifice of the Lamb: we live on what He gives us, we are His servants not out of fear but out of gratitude.

sens: White, crystalline mineral substance, extracted from the sea or mines, used to season and preserve food
Offering or provision delivered to the temple priests as part of the king's revenues
H4416.detail:
1. Salt is a well-known mineral substance used to add flavor to food and preserve it. In the three passages from the book of Ezra, salt is among the essential provisions: in Ezra 4:14, the royal officials eat "the salt of the palace," meaning they receive their sustenance from the royal treasury; in Ezra 6:9, salt is delivered daily to the priests along with wheat, wine, and oil for the burnt offerings; in Ezra 7:22, an indefinite quantity of salt ("as needed") is granted to the priests.
2. The expression "to eat the salt of the palace" (Ezra 4:14) means to receive one's sustenance from the king, to live off the royal treasury. It is an image of dependence and loyalty towards the one who nourishes. The officials who eat the king's salt owe loyalty to the king.
H4416.origine: The Hebrew word מְלַח (melach) simply designates salt, an essential substance in the ancient world for preserving food and for sacrifices. It comes from a root that expresses the idea of salting and preservation. Salt was rare, precious, and symbolized preservation and covenant.
H4416.emploi: The word "salt" appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in the book of Ezra (chapters 4, 6, and 7), during the reconstruction of the temple after the exile. It always refers to salt as a material provision delivered to the temple or as a symbol of the sustenance provided by the king. The context is administrative and economic: salt appears alongside wheat, wine, and oil, essential supplies for the functioning of worship and the maintenance of the priestly staff.
H4416.portee: Salt reminds us that God provides for the concrete needs of His people and His servants. In biblical language, "to eat someone's salt" expresses dependence on the one who nourishes: it is an image of gratitude and mutual obligation. For the Christian, this speaks of trust in divine Providence and gratitude towards God who sustains our lives each day.

sens: large salt lake bordering the Promised Land to the east
geographical limit and boundary of the land given by God to Israel
H4417G.detail:
1. The Salt Sea is the large salt lake located to the east of the Promised Land, today known as the Dead Sea. It is a vast body of water remarkably low and salty, which extends in the Jordan Valley (Genesis 14:3). It is mentioned as a major geographical landmark that the Israelites would have been well acquainted with.

2. The Salt Sea served as a natural boundary for the lands promised to Israel. In the passages delineating the territories, it precisely marks the eastern limit of the land: "your southern boundary shall start at the end of the Salt Sea, toward the east" (Numbers 34:3). It thus appears as a divine boundary, establishing the limits of God's gift to His people.
H4417G.origine: The Hebrew word melach means primarily "salt" — the white mineral substance that evaporates from salty waters. Here, the expression "Salt Sea" (yam melach) describes the lake by its most striking characteristic: its extremely salty, uninhabitable, and sterile water, which contrasts with the fresh water of the Jordan and the life-giving waters promised by God. It is a descriptive name, based on direct observation.
H4417G.emploi: The Salt Sea appears nine times in the Bible, primarily in Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua. It occurs in three contexts: first as a reference point of an ancient battle (Genesis 14:3), then as a key element of the tribal territory boundaries granted to Israel after the conquest (Numbers 34:3, 34:12; Deuteronomy 3:17; Joshua 12:3; Joshua 15:2, 15:5, 18:19), and finally during Joshua's crossing of the Jordan, where it marks the limit of the people on the move (Joshua 3:16). It is thus a stable, well-known geographical element that serves as a landmark for generations.
H4417G.portee: For the Christian reader, the Salt Sea reminds us that God gives His people boundaries, precise limits, and territorial promises. It invites us to contemplate God's faithfulness in maintaining His commitments from generation to generation, from Moses to Joshua. It is also a sign that the concrete geographical reality of the land was at the heart of the promise made to Abraham and his descendants.

sens: white crystalline substance, extracted from seawater or soil, used to season and preserve food
region of Palestine where significant biblical battles take place
H4417H.detail:
1. Salt is a well-known mineral substance: white, crystalline, extracted from natural saline sources. The Bible mentions it as valuable for preserving food and seasoning, but also as a symbol in religious rituals. Here, the word primarily refers to a famous valley in Palestine.
2. The Valley of Salt is a major geographical location south of the Dead Sea, where significant battles occur. David defeats eighteen thousand Edomites there (2 Samuel 8:13), just as Amaziah achieves a similar victory in the same place (2 Chronicles 25:11). It is a proper name for a region, but formed from the common word "salt," likely because saline deposits are abundant there.
H4417H.origine: The Hebrew word "melach" literally means "salt" and comes from the root that expresses bitterness or a sharp taste. Salt was extracted from the soil or natural saline sources in the ancient Near East. The Valley of Salt is named so because salt is naturally abundant there; it is an important mining region. In Greek, the word "hals" (ἅλς) has the same fundamental meaning.
H4417H.emploi: The word "salt" appears five times in the provided usages, always in the plural or followed by "valley." These five occurrences cover four centuries of biblical history: they describe three major battles won by David, Amaziah, and their generals against the Edomites (2 Samuel 8:13, 2 Kings 14:7, 1 Chronicles 18:12, 2 Chronicles 25:11, Psalms 60:2). The Valley of Salt is first a southern border of the territory of Judah, then a royal victory field where regional powers are measured. The number of warriors slain (ten to eighteen thousand) varies according to sources, but the valley itself remains a stable and prestigious geographical landmark.
H4417H.portee: This valley reminds the biblical reader that God granted victorious kings dominion over enemy peoples as a sign of His favor. The battles in the Valley of Salt mark the peak of Davidic and post-Davidic power. It is a place rich in national history, where strong Israel asserts its authority.

sens: White crystalline mineral substance, extracted from the sea or deposits, which seasons and preserves food
Element of purification and consecration of offerings in Israel's worship
Sign and guarantee of an unbreakable and everlasting covenant
What makes the land barren and uninhabitable when sown
What completely destroys and annihilates a place
H4417M.detail:
1. Salt is primarily the white crystalline mineral we know: it is added to food for seasoning, and Elisha uses it to "purify" a bitter water source (2 Kings 2:21). Job asks, "Is there any taste in the white of an egg?" — he speaks of the salt that gives flavor (Job 6:6).
2. In worship, salt was a mandatory part of offerings to the Lord. Leviticus 2:13 commands: "You shall put salt on all your offerings" — it is a rule of consecration, a mark of respect towards God.
3. Salt symbolizes the everlasting covenant: "It is an unbreakable covenant" (Numbers 18:19). Similarly, Jeroboam receives from the kingdom "a covenant of salt" (2 Chronicles 13:5), an image of something solid and durable, which does not corrupt like other things.
4. When Abimelech wants to destroy a city, he "sows salt" on its ruins (Judges 9:45) — salt makes the land barren and dead, preventing any future harvest.
5. Sowing salt on a devastated land is the definitive sign of annihilation: a curse that ravages everything (Deuteronomy 29:23; Zephaniah 2:9).
H4417M.origine: The Hebrew word מֶלַח comes from a root that evokes what is white and shiny. Sea salt was known in Israel since ancient times — the Dead Sea, in particular, provided it abundantly. The figurative meaning of an unbreakable covenant arises from the property of salt not to corrupt: a "covenant of salt" is a covenant that lasts, that never rots, unlike flesh or wood.
H4417M.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the Old Testament, mainly in three contexts: worship (offerings, purification), covenant (guarantee of permanence), and destruction (sterilization of enemy land). In Leviticus 2:13, salt accompanies every offering — it is an element of regular worship. In Numbers 18:19 and 2 Chronicles 13:5, the expression "covenant of salt" refers to a solid and everlasting covenant. In Judges 9:45 and Deuteronomy 29:23, sowing salt symbolizes definitive destruction: the land becomes cursed and barren. In 2 Kings 2:20-21, Elisha uses salt concretely to heal a source — here, salt purifies and restores.
H4417M.portee: Salt in the Bible teaches Christians two things: first, that consecration to God requires a visible and regular mark (the offering accompanied by salt); secondly, that the covenant with God is unbreakable and lasting, "of salt," meaning it never corrupts. Jesus will tell His disciples: "You are the salt of the earth" (Matthew 5:13) — an image of permanence and purity, of what preserves and seasons the world.

sens: Piece of worn and torn fabric
Clothing in tatters, reduced to rags
H4418.detail:
1. A rag is a piece of worn fabric, often torn or rotten. In Jeremiah 38:11, Ebed-Melech goes down to Jeremiah, a prisoner, "with worn rags and old rags" taken from the royal treasury: practically worthless rags, rendered useless for the king's house.
2. In a broader sense, a rag refers to clothing reduced to rags, made of pieces of damaged fabric. Jeremiah must place these rags "under his armpits, under the ropes" (38:12) so that the worn fabric protects his skin when he is pulled up from the cistern — it is an act of mercy towards a man at the end of his strength.
H4418.origine: The Hebrew word מֶלַח comes from a root that evokes the tearing and destruction of fabric. It properly designates what is frayed, what is in pieces. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew: it only appears in this passage from Jeremiah, applied to worthless rags.
H4418.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both in the same episode: Jeremiah 38:11-12. During the siege of Jerusalem, the prophet Jeremiah is thrown into a muddy cistern as a prisoner. Ebed-Melech, an officer of the king of Ethiopian origin, takes pity on him and pulls him out. To help him, he uses rags — remnants of fabric from the palace — which he places between the ropes and Jeremiah's body to protect him during the ascent. This is a poignant detail: only old worthless rags are available for this act of mercy.
H4418.portee: This passage shows us how God cares for even His most humiliated servants, and how He raises compassionate hearts — here, a stranger — to help them. The rags, though despicable, become an instrument of deliverance, reminding us that God uses the simplest means to accomplish His salvation.

sens: man who navigates and maneuvers a ship
sailor employed in maritime trade
one who knows the sea and its routes
H4419.detail:
1. The mariner is the skilled worker who navigates and maneuvers ships. He is the one who works on board to operate the vessel — a sailor in the most concrete sense of the term. In Jonah 1:5, the mariners of the ship carrying Jonah are afraid during the storm and cry out to their gods: these are the sailors who understand the danger and attempt to save their ship.

2. More broadly, he is a man of maritime commerce, integrated into the economic life of a major port city. In Tyre, a trading city of the Mediterranean, mariners work alongside pilots, merchants, and ship repairers (Ezekiel 27:9). They are part of the complex network that allows wealth to circulate.

3. He is also one who possesses experience in navigation and reading the sea. A mariner is not a passenger: he knows how to handle the oar, steer the helm, and read the sky and the waves. At the fall of Tyre, all these experienced men “handling the oar” come down from their ships, terrified (Ezekiel 27:29).
H4419.origine: The Hebrew word מַלָּח (mal.lach) comes from the root מלח (melah), which means “to be salty” or “saltiness.” This root immediately evokes the sea, as only the sea is salty. A mariner is thus literally “the man of salt” or “the man of the salty sea.” The Hebrew language constructs meaning in this way: the sailor is named by what characterizes his universe, the salty ocean. Other words from the same family designate salt itself or what is salty.
H4419.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of significant maritime navigation. Three occurrences are found in the prophetic vision of the fall of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:9, 27, 29), where Tyre, a great commercial power, loses all its mariners and sailors in the catastrophe — symbolizing the collapse of its wealth and influence. One occurrence is in Jonah 1:5, during the storm, where the mariners of the ship become the actors in the drama: they pray, they act, they throw the cargo into the sea. The meaning remains stable: it is always the experienced man of the sea, the one who works on the ship itself.
H4419.portee: For the biblical reader, the mariner represents the man confronted with the power of nature and his own weakness in the face of it. In Jonah, the mariners remind us that the Lord's storm shakes even those who have spent their lives on the water. In the vision of Tyre, they symbolize how the collapse of power reaches even the humblest artisans of commerce: no one can escape divine judgment. This word speaks of the ordinary man caught in events that surpass him.

sens: Salty character, presence of excess salt in land or soil
Sterility and desolation of land that has become unproductive
H4420.detail:
1. Salinity refers to the salty quality of land, particularly when salt accumulates in excessive amounts. This is a concrete reality: land soaked with salt can no longer nourish plants. Job 39:9 illustrates this: God makes the desert with its “salty” land the dwelling of the wild donkey, an animal capable of surviving in hostile conditions where no crops are possible.
2. By extension, salinity becomes the biblical image of spiritual and moral sterility, of divine abandonment. When God punishes a people, He transforms their “fertile land into salty land” (Psalms 107:34), signifying that blessing is withdrawn and the land becomes dead. Jeremiah 17:6 takes up the image: the one who turns his heart away from God dwells in “a salty and uninhabited land,” isolated and devoid of all abundant life.
H4420.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root “melach” (salt), and literally designates what is salty. In the ancient Near East, salt evoked infertility and death, in contrast to fresh water. Salted lands were once cursed or ruined — a powerful image to describe judgment or divine abandonment.
H4420.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to qualify a devastated land. In Job 39:9, it is the natural desert — hostile yet still a dwelling for God's creatures. In Psalms 107:34, it is a divine judgment: God transforms a fertile land into a salty desert to punish wickedness. In Jeremiah 17:6, it is the image of the fate of the isolated sinner. Each time, salinity symbolizes the absence of life, fertility, and blessing.
H4420.portee: This term reminds the believer that distance from God renders sterile all that should have been fruitful. Biblical salinity invites us to see that true fruitfulness — in life, relationships, and the soul — comes from the covenant with God, and that judgment is not merely an external punishment: it dries up from within.

sens: Armed conflict between nations, peoples, or kingdoms
Specific military engagement, combat, or battle
Action of fighting, battling with weapons
Set of operations, tactics, and military preparations
State of prolonged conflict or hostility
H4421.detail:
1. War is an armed conflict where entire peoples confront each other. In Genesis 14:2, kings declare war on each other, mobilizing their respective armies — this is the broadest sense of the word.
2. The battle refers to a specific engagement where combatants face each other on a field: in 2 Samuel 1:4, David learns that “a great number of men have fallen and perished” on the battlefield — it is the confrontation of a day.
3. Combat is the active action of fighting. In Jeremiah 4:19, the prophet hears “the sound of the trumpet, the cry of war” — the call to battle that resonates.
4. War includes all preparations and strategies: in 2 Chronicles 18:5, they ask, “Shall we go up to attack Ramoth in Gilead?” — this is contemplating the entire campaign with its plans.
5. War can also describe a lasting state of distrust or hostility: in Joshua 11:23, the land “was at rest and without war” — it is the peace regained after conflict.
H4421.origine: The word comes from an ancient Hebrew root (לחם, lham) which means “to fight” or “to battle.” The feminine form מִלְחָמָה adds the prefix “mi-” (which marks action or state). In the same family, we find the verb “to fight” and the word “soldier” (man of war). This Hebrew word is very ancient and very common: it fundamentally evokes the image of men opposing each other with weapons in hand.
H4421.emploi: The word מִלְחָמָה appears more than 300 times in the Hebrew Bible, wherever conflicts are recounted: wars between kings and peoples (Genesis 14), the conquest of Canaan (Joshua), Israel's struggles against its neighbors (1 Samuel, 2 Samuel). It designates either war in the broad sense (state of ongoing conflict) or a specific battle. Contexts vary: sometimes war is commanded by God as judgment or conquest; sometimes it results from pride or disobedience. The word also appears in a figurative sense: the Apostle Paul will speak of the spiritual warfare of the Christian (cited in Pauline usages). The Segond translates this single word into six French terms (war, combat, battle, to fight, to attack, soldier) depending on the precise context.
H4421.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the Bible does not hide the reality of violence and conflict in our world. It also teaches that true victory comes from God and not merely from military strength: God guides His peoples, sometimes commanding combat, sometimes granting peace. The reader discovers that strength without justice is vain, and that the Lord judges wars waged out of pride or injustice. Finally, in the New Testament, this vocabulary of combat becomes an image of the spiritual struggle of the believer against sin and evil.

sens: To leave a place of danger quickly to find safety
To escape from pursuit, a trap, or an enemy
To be saved, delivered from a threat or certain death
To let go, allow someone to flee
Figuratively: to snatch the soul from the realm of the dead, to save from perdition
H4422.detail:
1. To escape from a place: to flee quickly, to leave the walls of a city or the vicinity of danger. Lot is commanded, "Flee to the mountain, lest you be consumed" (Genesis 19:17) — he must leave as quickly as possible to live. David "had escaped from Keilah" (1 Samuel 23:13) means he left that city to escape Saul.
2. To escape pursuit or the hands of an enemy: to evade one who is hunting or capturing you. The army of Syria "escaped from your hands" (2 Chronicles 16:7): it managed to evade the control of King Asa.
3. To be saved from an imminent threat: to escape death or destruction. "Who can save his soul from the realm of the dead?" (Psalms 89:49) poses a question: can one truly save oneself from death? Jeremiah asks the fugitive, "What has happened?" (Jeremiah 48:19), seeking to know those who have escaped disaster.
4. To let someone flee or be delivered: to allow the person or life to be preserved. God "will save" the life of the righteous (Job 22:30), protecting him from danger.
5. To snatch life from perdition: to save the soul or people from spiritual or temporal ruin. God commands Jeremiah: "Save your souls! Flee!" (Jeremiah 51:6), for Babylon is about to fall.
H4422.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of slipping away, escaping quickly. It also gives rise to the word "escaped" (Jeremiah 48:19), referring to one who has saved himself. The central notion is rapid movement and evasion: one dodges, slips away from danger as one evades the grasp of an enemy. In biblical Hebrew, this verb can express both personal action (to flee oneself) and the action of another (to let go, to save someone else).
H4422.emploi: This verb appears 85 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives, the Psalms, and the prophets. It primarily describes concrete escapes: Lot fleeing Sodom, David fleeing Saul and Keilah. But it broadens its meaning to express any form of deliverance: escaping enemies, traps, or death itself. The Psalms use it to ask God to save the life of the faithful (Psalms 89:49, Psalms 107:20). The prophets use it to announce the salvation of a remnant (Joel 2:32, Isaiah 31:5) or the downfall of those who cannot escape (Isaiah 46:2: idols cannot save anyone). The word oscillates between the idea of physical escape and that of spiritual salvation.
H4422.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that true security does not come from our own strength or cunning to escape, but from the deliverance that only God can offer. In the face of peril, the righteous do not seek so much to flee as to seek divine protection. It also reveals the impotence of idols and creatures to save: only the Lord can snatch the soul from death and grant true salvation.

sens: Malleable earth used for construction
Material used to bind stones or bricks in walls
H4423.detail: 1. Clay is a malleable earth that can be shaped — here, that of a brick kiln. It is a soft material, easily excavated. In Jeremiah 43:9, the prophet asks the king of Judah to hide stones in the clay of the ground near Pharaoh's royal kiln: this is precisely the earthen or compact clay ground where he can dig and bury. 2. Clay also serves as mortar or cement to assemble bricks and stones: it binds and consolidates. In the context of construction at the time, clay was kneaded to make a binding coating.
H4423.origine: The Hebrew word מֶלֶט (melett) refers to clay, this natural earthen material. It likely comes from a root that evokes what can be shaped and compacted. The same material, omnipresent in the Near East, was used both to build foundations and walls (mixed with straw for bricks) and to bind them. It is the basic material of construction in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt.
H4423.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 43:9. The prophet entrusts King Zedekiah with a symbolic action: he must bury large stones in the clay of Pharaoh's Egyptian palace in Tahpanhes. These hidden stones represent the divine judgment that will fall upon this place. It is thus a context of prophecy and symbolic action, where clay is simply the material substrate, the ground in which one digs.
H4423.portee: This passage reminds us that God acts in the concrete history of peoples and places. Clay, a humble and ordinary material, becomes the ground where the divine word is inscribed — it is worked by the prophet as a sculptor works the earth, to announce God's judgments.

sens: Man from the time of exile and return
Gibeonite worker who helped rebuild the wall of Jerusalem
H4424.detail:
1. Melatia is a biblical character who lived during the Babylonian exile and the return of the Jews to the promised land. He appears only once in the Bible, briefly mentioned as one of the men who participated in the reconstruction work.

2. He is a Gibeonite, meaning a man from Gibeon, a city near Jerusalem. Alongside Jadon and the men of Gibeon and Mizpah, he works to rebuild the wall of Jerusalem damaged during the city's destruction by Nebuchadnezzar. His role shows the participation of local populations in the restoration of the holy city (Nehemiah 3:7).
H4424.origine: The name Melatia means "Jehovah has delivered" or "Yahweh has freed." It is composed of the divine name and a verb that evokes deliverance: this name expresses the hope of liberation, particularly appropriate for a man living at the time of the return from exile, when God brings His people back to their land.
H4424.emploi: Melatia is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Nehemiah 3:7. This is a passage where Nehemiah lists all the workers who contribute to the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the return from exile. Melatia is among these courageous builders, alongside figures like Jadon and the men from the cities of Gibeon and Mizpah. His appearance in this list of builders indicates that even non-Jews, like the Gibeonites, join in the effort to restore Jerusalem.
H4424.portee: Melatia represents the commitment of each individual, even humble and little known, in God's work. Although he is named only once and briefly, his participation in the wall of Jerusalem shows that every effort made to restore God's people has weight and value. For the believer, this reminds us that a life of service, even if unnoticed by the world, is counted and recognized by God.

sens: Ear of grain at the top of a cereal stalk
Head of wheat or barley ready to be harvested
H4425.detail: 1. The ear is the terminal part of the stalk of wheat or barley, which bears the grains tightly packed together. It is what the reaper cuts first, and it is also what can be hand-picked in a field when one is hungry. In Deuteronomy 23:25, the law of Moses allows the traveler to eat by plucking ears with his hand while passing through a field, but forbids him from doing a proper harvest with a sickle. 2. By extension, "ear" refers to the entire head of the cereal — the stalk crowned with grains — at the time of harvest, when the grains are swollen and golden, ready to be separated from their husk.
H4425.origine: The Hebrew word מְלִילָה likely comes from a root meaning "to rub" or "to grind," as one rubs the ears between their hands to extract the grains. The word thus literally designates what can be threshed by rubbing. It is a rural term, very concrete, related to the daily actions of the farmer and the reaper.
H4425.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in Deuteronomy 23:25, in a context of agrarian law. This law allows the poor and the traveler to pick a few ears by hand to satisfy their hunger, without it counting as theft — a practical application of love for one's neighbor and sharing. It is a simple, technical word that paints the rural life of Israel.
H4425.portee: This text teaches that even the right to property must give way to charity towards those who are hungry. Allowing the traveler to glean a few ears recognizes that everyone's essential needs take precedence over unlimited profit. For the Christian, it is a reminder that generosity towards the poor is not a favor, but a moral obligation inscribed in the law itself.

sens: Word or phrase difficult to understand, requiring reflection
Obscure saying or statement hidden in the words of the wise
Reproach, mockery, ridicule directed at someone
H4426.detail:
1. A riddle is primarily a word or phrase whose meaning is not immediate: one must search and reflect to understand it. In Proverbs 1:6, the young man seeks to "grasp the meaning of a riddle," that is, to decipher what the wise say in a veiled or indirect manner, with images and subtle turns of phrase.
2. The riddle can also be an enigmatic word, an obscure saying that hides a lesson or a truth under chosen words. The wise pronounce it not to confuse, but to instruct those who take the time to meditate on and understand it.
3. In Habakkuk 2:6, the riddle becomes mockery or reproach: the peoples will sing "riddles" — that is, taunts, hurtful words — against the one who unjustly accumulates wealth. Here, the riddle is no longer a lesson to meditate on, but an accusation formulated in the form of a riddle or a malicious saying.
H4426.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to speak in a roundabout way" or "to be obscure." It conveys the idea of a detour, a path that is not direct. The riddle is thus a word that takes a detour: it does not state things straightforwardly, but wraps them in images, wordplay, or veiled formulas.
H4426.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Proverbs 1:6, it designates one of the forms of wise speech — an obscure or enigmatic word that the young man must learn to decipher to become wise. In Habakkuk 2:6, it takes on a more aggressive nuance: it is a taunt, a mockery that the peoples direct at the tyrant or oppressor who accumulates wealth through violence. In both cases, it is a word that requires interpretation, but here it becomes a weapon of reproach.
H4426.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that biblical wisdom does not reveal its secrets at first reading: one must meditate, search, and reflect to grasp the meaning of the words of the wise. It is also a warning: those who oppress and accumulate through injustice will not go unpunished — future generations will sing taunts against them. Wisdom invites contemplation; the mockery of the peoples invites repentance.

sens: To exercise royal power, to govern a kingdom as a king or queen
To ascend to the throne, to become king or queen
To establish someone as king, to make them reign
To dominate, to impose oneself with authority
H4427A.detail:
1. To reign means to exercise royal power over a people and territory. It is the ongoing activity of a king who governs his kingdom. Example: "These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before a king reigned over the children of Israel" (Genesis 36:31).
2. To become king expresses the transition from the status of non-king to that of king, the accession to the throne. It is the decisive moment when someone begins to reign. Example: "Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he became king" (1 Kings 22:42).
3. To establish king or proclaim king (active form) means to put someone in power, to make them king by a deliberate decision or action. Example: "They proclaimed Solomon, son of David, king for the second time, anointing him before the Lord" (1 Chronicles 29:22).
4. By extension, to reign refers to any form of domination or absolute authority, like a power that imposes itself. It is the idea that royalty is a recognized and established domination.
H4427A.origine: The Hebrew verb מָלַךְ (malakh) comes from an ancient root that conveys the idea of being elevated, to rise, to stand at the top — the one who reigns is the one who is placed above. The noun מֶלֶךְ (mélekh) means "king" and derives directly from it. This word evokes the image of a person on a throne, dominating others by their elevated position and recognized authority. The root is common to ancient Semitic languages and always carries this idea of superiority and power.
H4427A.emploi: This verb appears more than 280 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical books: Samuel, Kings, Chronicles. It first describes foreign kings — the kings of Edom, Moab, Bashan (Genesis 36, Joshua 13) — and then especially the kings of Israel and Judah, from Saul to Zedekiah. The meaning nuances according to the context: it can mark the continuity of reign ("Solomon reigned for forty years"), the accession to the throne ("he became king"), the political establishment of a king by God or by the people ("he was proclaimed king"), or more figurative usages where a power or principle "reigns." The accounts of royal succession (David, Solomon, the dynasties of the North and South) are the main framework for this.
H4427A.portee: This word reminds us that royalty in the Bible is never a mere matter of force, but a function linked to the covenant with God. The kings of Israel reign only because God has established and chosen them. This teaches us that all power and authority come from God and that those who govern are accountable to Him for their reign. For the Christian, this vocabulary of reign prepares the way for understanding Jesus as King of kings, whose reign is eternal and perfect.

sens: Make a firm decision after reflection
Internally determine to act
H4427B.detail:
1. Make a firm decision after reflection — it is to deliberate within oneself, then to set a course of action. When Nehemiah says he has "resolved" to reprimand the nobles of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 5:7), he indicates that after contemplating the issue of usury against his brothers, he has made a firm determination and is preparing to act.
2. Internally determine to act — it is the moment when thought becomes a resolved will, where one mentally commits to doing something. The word emphasizes not the action itself, but this conscious decision that precedes and undergirds it.
H4427B.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of "deliberating" or "weighing in one's heart." It is related to words meaning "counsel" or "intention." The Aramaic used in the Bible (מְלֵךְ, melekh) directly means "counsel" or "advice," confirming that this verb expresses the process of reflection that leads to a resolution.
H4427B.emploi: This verb appears rarely in biblical Hebrew. Its only clearly attested use is in Nehemiah 5:7, where Nehemiah uses it to describe his decision to reprimand the leaders who oppressed the people through usury. The context shows that this is not an impulsive action: Nehemiah first listened to the complaints, then he "resolved" to intervene. The verb captures this moment of conscious determination that precedes public action.
H4427B.portee: This word reminds us that true Christian action begins with a mature inner decision. Like Nehemiah, who resolved to defend the poor against injustice, the believer is called to deliberate, then firmly determine to do what is right, without haste or hesitation.

sens: One who governs a kingdom, who holds supreme authority over a people and territory.
Military leader of a nation, who leads his troops into battle.
One who reigns by hereditary right or divine anointing over Israel.
Figure of authority and absolute power, worthy of fear and respect.
Title given to God or to one who governs the nations with wisdom.
H4428G.detail:
1. The king is the supreme leader of a kingdom: he governs, administers justice, and commands his people. In Genesis 14:1, several kings of the Middle East ally — this is a political and social reality of the time. The term designates both local petty chiefs and great monarchs.
2. The king is primarily a warrior leader who directs his armies into battle. When David is anointed king over Israel (1 Chronicles 14:8), the Philistines immediately seek him out: this is because a king can threaten his rivals on the battlefield.
3. In Israel, the king receives a special anointing from God — he is His anointed one, His representative. Deuteronomy 17:15 provides for a king that God will choose, showing that kingship is not a right but a charge entrusted.
4. The king embodies order, strength, and authority: he is respected, feared, and his orders are obeyed without question. In 2 Samuel 14:8, the king speaks and his words are executed immediately.
5. Jeremiah 10:7 calls God the "king of the nations": the term can express universal dominion and unparalleled wisdom, far beyond mere political reign.
H4428G.origine: The Hebrew word melekh comes from a root that means to govern, direct, establish order. Related words are found in Aramaic (melekh, identical form) and probably in other ancient Semitic languages. The fundamental image is that of one who holds the reins, who guides and organizes. The term is rooted in the political vocabulary of the ancient Near East and appears in contemporary Egyptian and Mesopotamian inscriptions, indicating that it designated a well-known and recognized reality.
H4428G.emploi: The word melekh appears about 2,000 times in the Old Testament, making it one of the most frequent words. It primarily designates the kings of foreign nations (Pharaoh of Egypt, the kings of Canaan in Genesis 14, the Ammonite kings in Numbers 21), and then gradually the kings of Israel and Judah, particularly Saul, David, and his descendants. The word also applies to God Himself as the eternal king. Its usage varies little: it is always a figure of supreme authority, but the context sometimes shows a just king, sometimes an unjust king, sometimes a king failing before God's enemies.
H4428G.portee: Understanding that God alone is the true king helps the believer to relativize human power. A king of Israel receives his charge from God and must answer for his management: he is merely a steward, not an owner. For the Christian, this image shows that all government exists by God's permission and must serve justice, not personal pride.

sens: A man of high rank at the royal court, father of Jerachmeel and Malkijah
A title or dignity attached to a function near the monarch
H4428H.detail:
1. The name "the King" (literally "the king") designates an officer or dignitary of King Zedekiah's court, living during the time of the divided monarchy of Judah. He is the father of Jerachmeel, who appears alongside two other royal officers (Seraiah and Shelemiah) when they receive the king's order to capture the prophet Jeremiah and his scribe Baruch (Jeremiah 36:26). He is a man of power and influence, invested with executive responsibilities.
2. The title "the King" can also designate the function or dignity itself: it is a nickname or designation that identifies him by his prominent role. His son Malkijah also has a connection to this dignity, as he possesses a cistern in the courtyard of the prison where Jeremiah will be thrown (Jeremiah 38:6), showing that the family enjoyed significant property and authority.
H4428H.origine: The Hebrew word "melekh" (מלך) literally means "king." In this context, it is used as a title or nickname rather than as the true proper name of the person. This is a common biblical practice: giving a powerful man or royal officer a title that reflects his status or function. The word comes from an ancient root meaning one who reigns or commands.
H4428H.emploi: The term "the King" appears only twice in the provided biblical usages, both in the book of Jeremiah, at the time of the fall of Jerusalem under Zedekiah. In Jeremiah 36:26, he is named as one of the royal officers tasked with capturing Jeremiah. In Jeremiah 38:6, he is identified by the name of his son Malkijah: he possesses the royal cistern where the prophet will be imprisoned. These two passages show him as a man of influence and trust at the throne, involved in the persecution of the prophet Jeremiah.
H4428H.portee: This character reminds the reader that opposition to the prophetic word also came from high-ranking court officials, not just from the king himself. It illustrates how the powerful often seek to silence those who proclaim divine judgment. It also shows that God protects His prophets despite human efforts to silence them: "the Lord hid them" (Jeremiah 36:26).

sens: Main road opened and maintained by the king or the state for travel and trade
Authorized passage through a territory without diverting or stealing
H4428I.detail:
1. The "royal road" is a major communication route constructed and maintained by royal authority, as opposed to small paths or private roads. It is wide, passable, and well-marked, making it the main route for traveling from one region to another. When the Israelites ask the king of the Ammonites: "we will follow the royal road, without turning to the right or to the left" (Numbers 20:17), they refer to this official and recognized way.
2. Figuratively, the royal road also symbolizes the legitimate and orderly right of passage: the Israelites promise to stay on the designated path, not to stray into private properties (fields, vineyards) or consume the resources of the land (wells). It is an agreement for peaceful passage, under control.
H4428I.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of royalty and reign. A "royal road" is literally the king's road, the one he uses or has built to assert his authority and facilitate exchanges in his kingdom. The expression emphasizes the importance and legitimacy of this path compared to other trails.
H4428I.emploi: This term appears twice in the Bible, in the two parallel passages where the Israelites, exiting Egypt, request passage through the lands of the king of the Ammonites (Numbers 20:17 and 21:22). In both cases, "royal road" designates the main and official path of the kingdom, which they commit to follow without deviation. The context shows that this road is a privilege and a recognized right of passage, distinct from small paths or rural properties.
H4428I.portee: This passage teaches us the importance of respect and legality in relations with others. The Israelites, although numerous and strong, politely request permission and commit to staying within the established framework. The "royal road" also evokes a just and orderly life: following the right path, the one marked by authority, is to walk with integrity and refuse tempting detours.

sens: One who exercises sovereign power over a kingdom
H4428J.detail: 1. The king is one who reigns over a people and territory, who governs and makes authoritative decisions. In Nehemiah 2:14, "the king's pool" refers to a water basin belonging to the sovereign of the Persian kingdom, likely built or maintained by his order — it is royal property, a place under his control.
H4428J.origine: The Hebrew word melekh (מֶלֶךְ) comes from a root that means "to advise" or "to reign"; it literally designates one who holds kingship, who possesses supreme authority. This word is very common throughout the Hebrew Bible to refer to the kings of Israel, Judah, and foreign sovereigns.
H4428J.emploi: The word melekh appears in the Bible to designate monarchs: kings of Israel and Judah, foreign kings (Egyptians, Assyrians, Babylonians, Persians), and even King Jesus in messianic prophecies. In Nehemiah 2:14, it refers to the Persian king under whose authority Nehemiah serves as governor. The context shows the pool as a royal possession, a property of the sovereign.
H4428J.portee: Understanding the word "king" helps grasp the political structure of the Bible: kings reign by God's delegation, and their power is subject to His will. This title also uniquely applies to Jesus Christ, the true eternal king.

sens: Deity worshiped by the Ammonites and other pagan peoples
False deity associated with child sacrifices
H4428K.detail: 1. This word designates a deity or supernatural power worshiped notably by the Ammonites and Moabites. In Zephaniah 1:5, he is called "king" — a title that underscores the domination attributed to him. The Israelites who turned away from him to worship their true God were renouncing this false deity. It is a word of judgment: Jeremiah denounces this impious worship among enemy peoples. 2. This "deity" was linked to abominable practices, particularly child sacrifice. Although this text does not explicitly mention it, the same deity is described elsewhere as demanding human offerings, which showed the spiritual darkness of this religion. That is why the name itself has become in the Bible a synonym for damnation and religious perversion.
H4428K.origine: This word is closely related to Molech (מֹלֶךְ), another form of the same pagan divine name. The Hebrew root evokes the idea of kingship or dominating power. The name was borne by a deity that several peoples of the Levant — Ammonites, Moabites, and even some apostate Israelites — revered and served. This worship was directly condemned by the Law of Moses as an abomination.
H4428K.emploi: This word appears three times in the Old Testament. In Zephaniah 1:5, the inhabitants of Jerusalem who bow down before the "king" (that is, Milcom) are denounced as unfaithful to the Lord. In Jeremiah 49:1 and 49:3, the prophet mocks the Ammonites who placed their trust in Milcom as their national defender — a vain trust, for their god could not save them from God's judgment. The word thus carries a connotation of condemnation: it is a false security, a worship doomed to failure.
H4428K.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that attachment to a false deity — whether ancient or modern — can only lead to ruin. Zephaniah shows that even within God's people, some have succumbed to the temptation of idolatry. It is a warning: true security and true power come only from the Lord, not from religious substitutes, however prestigious or promising they may seem.

sens: a famous valley near Jerusalem, in the Jordan region
H4428L.detail: 1. The valley of the King is a specific geographical location mentioned twice in the Hebrew Bible. Its name comes from the Hebrew *melek* which literally means "king", indicating that it was associated with royal authority or significant events involving kings. Genesis 14:17 designates it as the meeting place between Abram and the king of Sodom after the victory over Kedorlaomer. Two centuries later, Absalom had a monument built there (2 Samuel 18:18), confirming that this valley retained historical and symbolic importance for subsequent generations.
H4428L.origine: The Hebrew word *melek* means "king". In this topographical context, "valley of the King" evokes a place linked to royal authority or to major events involving kings. The proper name has become a geographical landmark, likely because royal meetings or monuments marked history there.
H4428L.emploi: The valley of the King appears twice in the provided biblical usages: in Genesis 14:17, where it serves as the meeting point between Abram and the king of Sodom after a decisive battle, and in 2 Samuel 18:18, where it is the site of the funeral monument that Absalom had constructed. These two occurrences establish it as a lasting territorial landmark, recognizable by contemporary readers and remembered as a place of passage and commemoration.
H4428L.portee: This valley reminds us that biblical geography is dotted with places of memory where the history of the patriarchs intertwines with that of the kings of Israel. It also testifies to human desire to leave a lasting mark of their passage on earth — Absalom hoping to perpetuate his name through a monument in the absence of heirs. It is a subtle call to consider what truly endures beyond our earthly endeavors.

sens: Benjamite from the time of the united monarchy, son of Micah and grandson of Mephibosheth
H4429.detail: Melech is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned twice in the genealogical lists of Chronicles. He is the second son of Micah (1 Chronicles 8:35 and 9:41), and he is the grandson of Mephibosheth, who was the son of Jonathan and grandson of King Saul. His name literally means "king" in Hebrew, but it is simply a name given to this man rather than a title.
H4429.origine: The Hebrew name מֶ֫לֶךְ (Melech) comes from the root מלך (malak), which means "to be king" or "to reign." It is the same word used to refer to the kings of Israel and Judah throughout the Bible. Parents often gave their children names evocative of power or dignity, and this name fits within this common practice in ancient Israel.
H4429.emploi: Melech appears only twice in the Bible, both in the first book of Chronicles in chapters 8 and 9, in parallel genealogical lists of the descendants of Benjamin. He is listed among the sons of Micah, alongside Pithon, Thaeréa (or Thachréa), and Ahaz. These genealogical lists trace the lineage of the tribe of Benjamin after the return from exile, going back to Saul and his family. Melech represents a generation of Benjamites living under the united monarchy, likely during the reigns of David or Solomon.

sens: One who reigns over a kingdom, who exercises supreme power
Royal authority, the function of governing a people
