Jacob enumerates Laban's injustices to justify his position — he does not simply say "always," but "ten times," supporting his grievance with a precise count. It is a reminder that our faith is rooted in real, countable, verifiable facts.

sens: Quantity of food or drink allocated to a person
Part of a sacrificial offering designated for the priest or the worshiper
Lot, destiny, or inheritance assigned by God
H4490.detail:
1. This word primarily designates a quantity of food or drink distributed to someone during a meal or celebration. In Nehemiah 8:12, after the reading of the Law, the people "went away to eat and drink, and to send portions" — meaning sharing food among neighbors and friends, a sign of communal joy.
2. In worship, it refers to the portion of a sacrificed animal reserved for the priest or the one offering the sacrifice. In Exodus 29:26, Moses "shall take the breast of the ram of consecration and wave it before the Lord: it shall be your portion" — the act of waving sanctified this part which legally belonged to the priest.
3. More broadly, the word expresses what is allotted to someone — their lot or inheritance. In Psalm 16:5, "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance" means that the faithful sees the Lord as their most precious possession, as their true wealth.
H4490.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to count" or "to enumerate." It designates what is distributed by counting — a measured and assigned share. The family of the word also includes verbs expressing the action of sharing or dividing. The meaning has enriched: beyond simple material division, it evokes everything one receives from fate or divine will.
H4490.emploi: This word appears 13 times in the Old Testament, mainly in law texts (Exodus, Leviticus) and historical accounts (Samuel, Chronicles, Esther, Nehemiah). It is frequent in passages about sacrifices: the priest receives a "portion" of the offered animal, which is a right established by the Law (Leviticus 7:33). It is also found in accounts of festive meals: in Esther 9:19 and 9:22, during the Feast of Purim, the Jews "send portions to one another" to celebrate their deliverance. Finally, it can express a personal gift: in 1 Samuel 1:5, Elkanah "gave Hannah a double portion" because he loved her — here, "portion" is a mark of affection.
H4490.portee: This word roots the reader in a tangible reality: God does not despise bread, shared food, the joy of a meal. He even claims them for Himself (in the sacrificial portion) and sanctifies them. Psalm 16:5 invites us to see beyond: our "true portion" is not in fleeting wealth, but in God Himself. It is an invitation to recognize that we possess nothing by right — everything is grace.

sens: the way to drive a chariot or mount
the characteristic style of a person on horseback or in a chariot
the pace, the way of moving
H4491.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the concrete manner of directing a chariot or horses — the skill, speed, the gestures of the driver. In 2 Kings 9:20, the watchman recognizes Jehu from afar by his "manner": he drives with such violence and boldness that it is his personal signature.
2. By extension, it refers to the characteristic style or pace of a person: how they present themselves, how they act, what makes them recognizable to others — here, Jehu's impatience and boldness, who drove "in a reckless manner."
H4491.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to drive" or "to lead." It evokes the image of a chariot driver: this was a prestigious activity in the Ancient Near East, requiring strength, courage, and experience. The word belongs to the family of terms related to direction, command, and self-control.
H4491.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Kings 9:20. It is a technical term from the military and royal world: only leaders, warriors, or kings drove war chariots. Its use here emphasizes that Jehu had such a violent and recognizable driving style that the sentinels distinguished him from other chariots from afar. It is a detail that reveals his impetuous character and boldness.
H4491.portee: This word reminds us that our actions, our way of living and acting make us recognizable to those who watch us. Just as Jehu's manner revealed his recklessness, our conduct reveals what we are internally. It is an invitation to examine how we present ourselves to the world and to those who observe us.

sens: A fissure, a crevice in the rock of a mountain
A natural underground cavity, a cave or hollow in the ground
A hidden refuge where one can take shelter
H4492.detail:
1. A ravine is a fissure or deep crevice in the rock of a mountain, a place where the stone has naturally parted. It is the image of rugged and difficult terrain.

2. It is also an underground cavity, a cave or hollow in the ground — spaces carved by erosion or holes that can be dug for hiding. In Judges 6:2, the children of Israel would retreat precisely into these ravines of the mountains to escape the raids of the Midianites: the ravine becomes a natural shelter.

3. Figuratively, the ravine designates a refuge, a place where one can take shelter from danger. It is a secluded place, difficult to reach, ideal for fleeing from powerful enemies.
H4492.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to dig" or "to be hollow." It evokes the image of what is emptied, what forms a cavity — whether a fissure in the rock or a hole in the ground. The root refers to the idea of digging and inner emptiness.
H4492.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Judges 6:2. It designates the natural refuges where the Israelites hid from Midianite oppression. The context shows people forced to flee, compelled to live withdrawn in the most inaccessible places — the ravines, caves, fortified rocks — to survive. The word paints a situation of distress and resistance: one does not inhabit a ravine by choice, but by necessity.
H4492.portee: This passage reminds us that even in the darkest hours, when believers are cornered and without apparent resources, God offers places of refuge. The hidden ravines of Judges 6 spiritually foreshadow this divine protection in times of oppression. It comforts us: in our trials, there is always a place, a strength where we can take shelter.

sens: Movement of the head back and forth or up and down, expressing doubt, mockery, or contempt
H4493.detail: 1. Nodding is a gesture of the head that expresses rejection or mockery. In Psalm 44:15, the nations nod their heads at Israel to mock and insult him, as one would do in the presence of someone who evokes disdain.
H4493.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning to move, sway, or wobble. This root evokes any repeated and involuntary movement of the head. The noun מָנוֹד specifically refers to this type of expressive gesture.
H4493.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 44:15. It describes a gesture of mockery directed at God's people in a context of dishonor and contempt. It is an outward sign of the social and spiritual rejection that the nations direct toward Israel.
H4493.portee: This word reminds us how contempt and mockery can be expressed physically, and how God's people can be humiliated by their enemies. For the believer, it illustrates the sufferings and humiliation that God's people endure, and invites trust despite the world's rejection.

sens: Place where one can settle, stop
State of calm, absence of agitation
Security, stability, and established peace
Fulfillment of what is sought or expected
H4494.detail: 1. Rest is primarily a physical place to find refuge and stop: the dove found "no place to set the sole of her foot" (Genesis 8:9) — she was seeking a solid surface to rest on after the flood. 2. It is also the inner state that accompanies this halt: a calming, a relaxation of body and mind after effort or fear. 3. By extension, it is lasting security, stability: Judah in exile "finds no rest" (Lamentations 1:3) means that he cannot live in peace, that he is always threatened, without a stable foundation. 4. Finally, it is the fulfillment of a quest: Naomi wants to "secure rest" for Ruth (Ruth 3:1), meaning to give her a husband, a home, an established and happy life. The word paints each time the image of an end to turmoil.
H4494.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of stopping, ceasing. It designates both the place where one stops and the state that results from it — the tranquility found there. The ark itself, once the waters recede, finally has "a place of rest" (1 Chronicles 6:31): it can remain still, it is no longer tossed about. It is a very concrete word in Hebrew.
H4494.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible. Genesis 8:9 shows it in its most physical sense: a place where a living being can settle. Deuteronomy 28:65 and Lamentations 1:3 use it to describe the absence of peace — a curse or tragedy where one can never rest. Ruth 3:1 uses it to evoke a happy marriage that establishes a woman in life. 1 Chronicles 6:31 and Isaiah 34:14 maintain the image of a dwelling place. The word thus moves from the physical (a place to settle) to the spiritual and moral (peace, security, established happiness).
H4494.portee: This word reminds the believer that God offers rest — not just a pause, but a stable and secure state of being. For the Israelites, rest primarily represented entry into Canaan, the end of the desert. For every Christian, it evokes the calming of the heart in God, the cessation of spiritual wandering, and life finally established according to the Father's will.

sens: Inhabitant of Zorah, of the tribe of Dan
Father of the judge Samson
Man who received a visit from an angel announcing the birth of his son
H4495.detail: Manoach is a man of the tribe of Dan living in Zorah before the establishment of the monarchy in Israel (Judges 13:2). He is best known as the father of Samson, the judge whose birth God had planned. His wife being barren, Manoach himself becomes the witness of a remarkable divine intervention: an angel appears to him to announce the conception and birth of his son, with the specific conditions that he must observe (Judges 13:12-13). Manoach plays a humble but significant role in this narrative: he asks questions of the angel, seeks to understand what will happen, and ultimately recognizes the divine presence when the angel disappears in the flame of the altar (Judges 13:20).
H4495.origine: The name Manoach means "rest" in Hebrew, derived from a root expressing calm and tranquility. This name may reflect the hope of the parents: he would bring rest after years of barrenness and disappointment.
H4495.emploi: Manoach appears exclusively in the account of Samson in the book of Judges, chapter 13 and chapter 16, for a total of 14 occurrences. He is presented as a pious man who prays for a child (Judges 13:8) and who, when the angel appears to him, asks a series of practical questions: what must he observe, what is the name of the angel (Judges 13:12, 13:17). With his wife, he recognizes the divine manifestation when the angel disappears in the flame rising from the altar (Judges 13:20). At the end of the narrative, he buries Samson after his death (Judges 16:31).
H4495.portee: Manoach illustrates the faith of an ordinary Israelite parent in the face of God's action. He does not understand everything, he asks questions, but he obeys and bows before what exceeds his understanding. His story invites the reader to recognize that God sometimes acts in surprising ways and that our role is to humbly welcome what He reveals, even when we do not grasp all the details.

sens: Exert a violent and continuous pressure until something or someone is crushed
Pursue relentlessly, reduce to helplessness
H4496G.detail:
1. The verb describes the physical action of crushing, pressing with force until destroying or breaking what is at hand. It is a violence applied relentlessly. In Judges 20:43, the Israelites "crush" Benjamin: they press him, pursue him without giving him any respite, as one crushes something crushing.
2. Figuratively, it means to incapacitate someone, reducing them to helplessness through continuous and inexorable pressure. The word suggests a lack of mercy, a total domination that annihilates the capacity for resistance or even rest of the opponent.
H4496G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to press," "to push with force." It is related to the idea of continuous and overwhelming pressure. The structure of the word in Hebrew makes it an action verb that suggests the repetition or persistence of the gesture: one does not crush just once, one crushes continuously.
H4496G.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 20:43, during the account of the terrible civil war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin. The Israelites pursue the fleeing Benjaminites without giving them a moment's rest, literally crushing them until they are annihilated. The use of the verb "crush" rather than "fight" or "pursue" emphasizes the merciless brutality and complete crushing of the enemy.
H4496G.portee: This word reminds the reader of the terrible cost of internal violence within a people. The crushing of Benjamin illustrates how sin and divine justice can produce fratricidal wars that destroy without remission. It is a warning against systematic cruelty, even when it claims to serve justice.

sens: A place where one can stop and rest
The state of calm and tranquility resulting from rest
The peace and security offered by God
A refuge, a safe asylum
H4496H.detail:
1. A place where one can stop and rest: it is primarily a physical location where someone ceases to travel or work to regain strength. Genesis 49:15 speaks of the "place where he rests" as a pleasant spot. Ruth 1:9 asks the Lord to grant each one "rest": it is the tranquil home of marriage.
2. The state of calm and tranquility resulting from rest: beyond the physical place, the word denotes inner peace, the absence of disturbance. Psalms 116:7 invites the soul to "rest" after the Lord has done good. It is a condition of the mind and heart.
3. The peace and security offered by God: in the Old Testament, "rest" becomes a divine gift. Psalms 95:11 mentions the Lord's "rest" as a blessing intended for His people, but which some refuse. God's rest represents the ultimate blessing and deliverance.
4. A refuge, a safe asylum: Isaiah 32:18 speaks of "quiet places" where the people dwell in safety, protected from enemies and dangers. It is a stable and assured dwelling.
H4496H.origine: The word comes from the root נוּחַ (nuach), which means "to rest, to settle down." This root evokes the image of something that ceases to move and gently settles, like a dove landing after its flight. It appears in Genesis when Noah's ark "rests" on the mountains (Genesis 8:4). The word ménoukhah is the action noun derived from this root: it denotes the state or place resulting from rest. The notion of stability and peace is deeply inscribed in it.
H4496H.emploi: This word appears 21 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, historical books, and the prophets. In the narratives (Genesis, Ruth, 1 Kings), it describes places or moments of concrete rest. In the Psalms (95, 116, 132), it denotes the rest that the Lord offers His people as a sign of His blessing and covenant. In the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah), rest becomes more spiritual: it is the promise of lasting peace, but also judgment against those who refuse it. In 1 Chronicles 22:9, Solomon is called a "man of rest" because he will reign without continual wars. The word thus oscillates between physical rest and spiritual blessing, between place and state of the soul.
H4496H.portee: This word invites the believer to understand that rest is not only a physical need but a gift from God. It reminds us that God wants to offer His people a stable and definitive peace (Psalms 95), which is fulfilled in Jesus Christ in the New Testament. Meditating on God's rest encourages us to cease our striving, to trust in His deliverance, and to seek first His kingdom, knowing that He will grant us the peace that surpasses all understanding.

sens: To have an inner conviction about something
H4497.detail: 1. The word expresses the idea that someone forms an inner conviction, often erroneous or presumptuous, about their own condition or status. In Proverbs 29:21, the servant treated too gently ends up "believing" — convincing himself — that he is a son, meaning that he deserves a high position that he does not actually have.
H4497.origine: The precise etymology of the word is debated. It seems related to a root expressing inner feeling or personal conviction. In Hebrew, this verb is rare and its exact history remains obscure in ancient sources, which explains why translators hesitate about its primary meaning.
H4497.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 29:21. It is used in a context of family and educational wisdom: the warning that treating a servant too indulgently from childhood creates false convictions about his social status. This rarity makes its exact meaning difficult to establish with certainty, but the context of the proverb clearly suggests a personal conviction.
H4497.portee: This passage teaches practical wisdom about education and the limits of indulgence: unlimited affection can create a distorted view of one's condition and place in the one who receives it. It is a lesson on the balance between kindness and clarity regarding each person's roles and responsibilities.

sens: A place to seek safety from danger
The act of fleeing, escaping
Divine or human protection offered to one seeking shelter
H4498.detail:
1. A refuge is a physical place where one takes shelter from a threat. It is a high retreat, a safe place to which to flee. In 2 Samuel 22:3, the psalmist declares that God is his refuge, the safe place where he finds protection against violence.
2. The word also evokes the action of fleeing, the very movement of escaping danger. It is the urgent need to leave, to quit a threatened place. In Jeremiah 46:5 and Amos 2:14, we see warriors who have no refuge left — they can no longer escape.
3. More profoundly, the refuge is the protection that someone offers to one in distress. It is active help, assistance. Jeremiah 16:19 shows the refuge as the strength of the one who grants it: the Lord is the refuge of the prophet in the day of distress.
H4498.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to flee" or "to escape." It is a noun formed to designate the place or act of fleeing. In biblical Hebrew, this family of words expresses the idea of rapid movement to escape danger. The word belongs to the vocabulary of the psalms and the prophets, who often speak of God as the only true refuge.
H4498.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the psalms and the prophets. In 2 Samuel 22:3, Psalms 59:17, and Jeremiah 16:19, the refuge is God Himself: it is a confession of faith. In Job 11:20, Psalms 142:5, and Jeremiah 25:35, "having a refuge" or "losing all refuge" denotes the concrete situation of the unfortunate: the lost refuge is the end of all help. In Jeremiah 46:5 and Amos 2:14, the warriors "have no refuge" — they cannot flee, they are trapped.
H4498.portee: The refuge speaks to the believer of his security in God. When the psalmist calls God his refuge, he affirms that only God can protect him from all that threatens him. This word reminds us that true refuge is not a place we create for ourselves, but one that God offers. For the Bible reader, it conveys the urgency of seeking shelter in God when fear fills the heart.

sens: Action of fleeing quickly in the face of danger
Route, disorderly retreat
Movement of panic in response to a threat
Hasty escape
H4499.detail:
1. The word denotes the concrete action of fleeing quickly, often without any real pursuit: in Leviticus 26:36, those who survive are seized by such panic that they "flee as one flees from the sword" at the mere sound of a leaf, even though no one is actually pursuing them. It is fear that makes them run, not an immediate danger.
2. The word also evokes a retreat, a hasty departure from a place: in Isaiah 52:12, it refers to not leaving "in flight," meaning not to leave Jerusalem in the panic and disorder of those fleeing the enemy, but rather with dignity and confidence, for God will go before the people.
H4499.origine: The Hebrew word מְנוּסָה comes from the root נוס (nus), which means "to flee," "to escape." This root evokes the idea of moving quickly to escape danger. The suffix -ה indicates the abstract nominal form: not a single act, but the action or state of fleeing in general.
H4499.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe a flight characterized by fear or urgency. In Leviticus 26:36, it illustrates the extreme terror inflicted by God as punishment: the mere agitation of the wind is enough to send those whose hearts have lost all confidence fleeing. In Isaiah 52:12, the word plays an inverse pedagogical role: it reminds the exiled people not to leave in flight like defeated ones, but to walk confidently, for God Himself is their guide and protector.
H4499.portee: This word shows that fear is the true enemy: it causes flight even without a real threat, it paralyzes confidence. For the Christian, it calls to not be governed by panic, but to walk in faith in God who goes before us. In Isaiah, it teaches us to leave our old habits and servitudes, not through frantic flight, but through quiet trust in the One who leads us.
